gist: Firefighters and control room staff were stretched dangerously thin during this summer's wildfires.
A parliamentary report revealed that firefighters struggled with water supplies and poor preparation amid drought.
A summit is being held to address climate resilience and future wildfire preparedness in Wales.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: This summer's record-breaking heat and drought fuelled serious wildfires across the UK. Fire services faced unprecedented demand, with crews managing multiple major fires at once and control rooms handling thousands of calls. Firefighters reported severe shortages of staff, appliances, proper equipment, and water supplies due to low pressure and depleted natural sources.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The crisis exposed critical weaknesses in the UK's resilience and preparation for extreme weather. Experts warned that firefighters and the public were knowingly put at risk as climate breakdown increases the frequency and severity of wildfires, placing an unsustainable burden on emergency services and water networks.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Leaders and key partners are gathering for a climate change and resilience summit in Merthyr Tydfil to develop future actions. A UK wildfire conference is also scheduled in Leeds, while MPs have called on the government to establish statutory responsibilities for water companies during major fire incidents.

gist: Two AI-discovered vulnerabilities in the PHP language caused widespread website outages today.
The 20-year-old bugs allow unauthenticated remote code execution and full server control.
Government agencies, gaming platforms and major websites took systems offline as precautions.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Two critical vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language used by a large majority of websites. AI models helped identify the flaws, which allow hackers to execute remote code without an administrator login. Organisations worldwide took their sites offline, and security firms warned of emerging attacks.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The flaws affect a massive share of the internet, including Wikipedia, WordPress sites, and various government agencies. Attackers could gain full control of servers, accessing sensitive databases, passwords and cryptographic certificates.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Website administrators and hosting services need to check their PHP versions and update to fixed releases immediately. Sites running unsupported older versions must upgrade, while vulnerable servers without an immediate patch should be taken offline.

fivew: Websites, government agencies, and security researchers including Wiz and OpenAI.

Organisers blamed unexpected issues and a last-minute participant surge for the logistical strain.
Concerns were raised about the contractor GL Events cutting corners, while officials defended them.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Asian Games in Nagoya and Aichi Prefecture suffered from diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. Organisers skipped building an athletes' village to cut costs, housing participants in hotels and container units instead. Last-minute additions swelled participant numbers to 17,000, forcing the use of a cruise ship. Further mishaps included transport errors, wrong national anthems, flag errors, and temporary bans on officials.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Experts warned that the chaotic events could damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate future sporting events. Local media criticised the contractor GL Events for aggressively cutting corners and lacking trained staff, though organisers defended the firm's experience.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Experts hope organisers will learn from the problems to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future. Meanwhile, glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, prompting official apologies.

sections.text: Judges in England and Wales will be granted powers to confine offenders to their cells for up to three weeks and block social visits if they refuse to attend sentencing hearings. timeline.text: Proms, parties and gender politics: amazing photos from American dancefloors – and what they tell us about a changing nation

gist: A new Taschen book compiles dance-themed photographs from the historic Life magazine archive.
The images chronicle shifts in American culture, gender politics, race relations and individualism.
Featured moments include Cold War tensions, iconic performers, high school proms and global dance crazes.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Taschen published LIFE. Let’s Dance, a book drawing on dance photography from the archive of Life magazine, which ran weekly between 1936 and 1972. The collection covers social dancing across ballrooms, clubs, proms and parties, showcasing styles from the waltz and lindy hop to the twist. It also documents renowned performers, including George Balanchine, Margot Fonteyn, Rudolf Nureyev, Whitey’s Lindy Hoppers, the Rockettes, and actors filming the movie musical Can-Can.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The archive reflects broader shifts in twentieth-century American society. The transition from structured couple dancing to freeform movement captured emerging gender politics and individualism. Photographs also traced shifting racial dynamics, from segregated venues and newly desegregated schools to the mainstream adoption of Black and Latin American styles. In addition, dance intersected with Cold War tensions, from Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev criticising Hollywood routines to comparisons between American and Soviet schools.

fivew: Publisher Taschen released the book featuring work from Life magazine's photographers.
A collection of dance-themed photographs from the Life magazine archive has been published in a book.

The archive reflects major twentieth-century American social changes, gender politics, race relations and Cold War tensions through dance.

gist: New York City Council voted to ban horse-drawn carriages by June 2028.
The legislation, named Romanch's Law, follows safety concerns and animal welfare complaints.
Carriage drivers and the Transport Workers Union strongly oppose the ban, citing job losses.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The New York City Council voted to pass a ban on horse-drawn carriages, set to start in June 2028. The measure, known as Romanch's Law, follows safety and animal welfare concerns, notably the death of a teenager this summer after a runaway carriage incident.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The decision ends a traditional tourist activity operating for over 160 years. While animal rights groups and supporters welcome the move to protect public safety and animal welfare, carriage drivers and the Transport Workers Union warn it will destroy livelihoods and threaten multi-generational family enterprises.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Operations will continue until June 2028, with a transition plan proposed to help workers find new employment. Meanwhile, the Transport Workers Union has stated it plans to pursue legal action in federal court against the legislation.

sections.text: Startup Nirva announced a $25 million pre-Series A round, adding to an earlier $8 million raised this year, bringing its total raise to $33 million. sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A 16-year-old former student armed with a shotgun entered Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon. He shot six people, killing three students and a teacher, before a parent fatally shot him. Teacher Becky Drury was shot while trying to close her classroom door and pretended to be dead to survive.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The tragedy left a community mourning and schools reopening with heavy police presence. Drury released a statement to correct contradictory reports about her actions during the incident.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Public schools in Bend began reopening this week with dozens of officers welcoming students back to classes. The shooting remains under investigation by police.

sections.text: Premature twins Raghad and Raad fled with their family on foot for three days as fighting surged in Yemen. Arriving at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, they were diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition driven by conflict and poverty.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The collapse of an informal ceasefire has intensified the conflict, displacing thousands and cutting off aid to hundreds of thousands of people, leaving vulnerable children caught in the middle of a hunger crisis.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Hospital staff continue treating critical cases under severe constraints, while displaced families face ongoing poverty, lack of resources, and the risk of recurring illness for their children.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Indian actor and director Nana Patekar died aged 75 of a heart attack. Known for his intense performances and versatility across heroic and villainous roles, he rose to international prominence in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay! and starred in major Bollywood hits including Parinda and Krantiveer. His later career involved philanthropic work through the Naam Foundation, alongside a return to screen acting after facing sexual harassment allegations raised by Tanushree Dutta.

sections.text: Patekar was regarded as a towering figure in Indian cinema, remaining alongside Irrfan Khan as the only performer to win Filmfare’s best actor, best supporting actor and best villain awards. His rougher edges and naturalistic style brought street realism to Bollywood. However, accusations made by his former co-star Tanushree Dutta in 2018 kickstarted India’s #MeToo movement, permanently altering the conversation around his legacy.

articles.title: Elon Musk says Tesla will sell 5 million cars by 2030 — math says otherwise
articles.standfirst: On Tesla's earnings call Wednesday, Elon Musk made one of his patented pie-in-the-sky predictions that typically sends his fans into paroxysms of ecstasy: 5 million vehicle deliveries by 2030. "We were aiming for 5 million vehicles a year by approximately 2030," he said.

timeline.text: Elon Musk says Tesla will sell 5 million cars by 2030 — math says otherwise

gist: Elon Musk predicts Tesla will achieve 5 million annual vehicle deliveries by 2030.
This target requires a daunting 25 percent compound annual growth rate.
Meeting this goal appears unrealistic due to factory limits and regulatory hurdles.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: During an earnings call, Elon Musk stated that Tesla is aiming to sell 5 million vehicles a year by approximately 2030. This projection is actually a downgrade from his previous 2020 prediction of 20 million annual sales by 2030. Tesla has experienced back-to-back delivery declines, falling from a peak in 2023.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Achieving the 2030 goal requires a 25 percent compound annual growth rate. However, Tesla relies heavily on just two vehicles, discontinued older models, faced declining sales, and abandoned plans for a cheaper mass-market electric vehicle. Furthermore, reaching 5 million cars demands doubling current factory space, and the alternative strategy relies heavily on unapproved autonomous robotaxis.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Tesla hopes to launch unsupervised Full Self-Driving and deliver steering-wheel- and pedal-less Cybercabs. However, these plans depend on government approvals, which take time and face regulatory scrutiny.

gist: Certificate authority eMudhra is withdrawing from the global TLS business.
The decision follows the discovery of eight weak intermediate TLS credentials.
The company cited compliance costs and social media scrutiny as factors.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Certificate authority eMudhra issued eight intermediate TLS credentials with extremely weak private keys. Researchers revealed the defect, allowing anyone to crack the keys in milliseconds and generate trusted TLS certificates. Following this incident, eMudhra announced it is withdrawing from the global SSL/TLS business.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The compromised certificates were so defective that they could be used to mint certificates for any website or mail server, threatening trust across major browsers and various devices.

fivew: Certificate authority eMudhra is dropping out of the TLS business.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Items belonging to the Kilda fishing boat were recovered from an area off the coast near Port of Ness. The vessel disappeared off the north coast of the Isle of Lewis on 13 October with three crew members on board. The body of one crewman was recovered early the next morning, while the search continues for the remaining two. Police Scotland's marine and dive unit carried out the search, and an MAIB exclusion zone was established.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Police described the search as a complex operation as efforts continue to find the missing crew and provide answers for their families. A GoFundMe page has raised more than £148,000 to support the affected families.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Marine Accident Investigation Branch exclusion zone is set to be lifted. Police inquiries and efforts with partners are ongoing, while the public has been urged not to put themselves at risk by conducting independent searches.

Ministers are considering tougher local restrictions and product bans when fire risk is high.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Following a record-breaking summer of destructive blazes, the UK government announced measures to tackle wildfires. Plans include deploying military aircraft to remote terrain, establishing an AI Cobra unit within the National Situation Centre to detect fires faster, and providing £45m for specialised personal protective equipment for firefighters.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Over half of 29 surveyed fire services lacked wildfire-specific gear, leaving firefighters with heavy building-fire kit that risks overheating and fails to block carbon monoxide. Earlier this month, parliamentary committee members identified national weaknesses in aerial resources, water access, and coordination during major wildfire incidents.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Tech companies, fire chiefs, and local leaders will attend a wildfire resilience summit. Ministers are considering tougher local restrictions or product bans during high-risk periods. A £25m peatland restoration scheme and farmer funding to fireproof land will run from April 2027 to April 2029.

fivew: Andy Burnham and defence secretary Wes Streeting presented the government plans.
The UK government announced new wildfire measures including military aircraft deployment, an AI detection unit, and funding.
The announcements were outlined ahead of a summit on Friday, following blazes earlier in the summer.
The measures cover the UK, with specific peatland funding focused on England.
The plans respond to a record-breaking summer of devastating blazes and identified weaknesses in wildfire preparedness.

gist: A personalised mRNA vaccine combined with immunotherapy reduced melanoma recurrence or death by 42%.
The phase III clinical trial involved 1,137 patients whose tumours had been surgically removed.
Drugmakers Moderna and MSD are testing the approach against other types of cancer.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: In a trial of 1,137 adults with resected melanoma, the personalised mRNA vaccine intismeran combined with the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab cut the risk of cancer returning or death by 42% after two years. Additionally, 82% of patients receiving the combined treatment remained alive and recurrence-free, compared with 70% taking immunotherapy alone.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: It is the first individualised cancer vaccine to show positive phase III trial results. The vaccine targets up to 34 unique genetic mutations from a patient's tumour to train the immune system to prevent cancer returning.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Results will be presented at a Madrid conference and published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Manufacturers MSD and Moderna are seeking regulatory approval and testing the vaccine against lung, bladder and kidney cancers.

quotes.text: a foundational shift in our approach to cancer
quotes.role: medical director at the Melanoma Institute Australia

gist: Corey Lewandowski faces a criminal investigation regarding his role at the Department of Homeland Security.
Investigators are examining whether he personally profited from agency contracts during his tenure.
His lawyer denies any wrongdoing by his client.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Department of Justice is conducting a criminal investigation into Corey Lewandowski, a former top aide at the Department of Homeland Security, over allegations that he profited from his governmental position and signed contracts without proper legal authority.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Investigations involving individuals close to Donald Trump are uncommon, and the probe stems from concerns that temporary federal advisers may have misused their authority for personal financial gain.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The criminal investigation continues following a referral from the inspector general's office, though federal prosecutors have not yet issued subpoenas or formal legal demands.

timeline.text: Denmark to ban mink farming in government U-turn

gist: Denmark will ban mink farming following a government decision.
The country previously sought an exemption from an EU-wide ban.
Only seven mink farms remain operating in the country.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Danish government reversed its previous position and dropped plans to seek an exemption from an impending EU ban on keeping mink. The prohibition takes effect next August, followed by a two-year transition period ending in August 2029.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The decision prioritises animal welfare over a traditional business. Denmark was historically the world's leading producer of mink fur, but the sector shrank significantly after a coronavirus outbreak triggered a mass cull.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The remaining seven mink farms will phase out operations during the two-year transition period, and final closure costs are yet to be determined.

fivew: Denmark decided to ban mink farming instead of pursuing an exemption from an EU prohibition.
The government reversed its decision on Friday, with the ban starting next August and ending in 2029.
Officials chose to prioritise animal welfare and societal benefit.

quotes.text: A business should not continue just because it has existed for a long time.
It is absolutely the right decision not to apply for a special scheme for mink breeding in Denmark

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Two museums in Glasgow have taken Egyptian mummified remains off public display. gist: Jobseekers worry about automated recruitment tools and bias.
Many workers are unaware they can request human reviews.
Recruiters note a surge in AI-written applications.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Jobseekers face automated rejections and growing concerns over AI recruitment tools. A campaign called Reject the Rejections highlights that many workers do not know their legal right to challenge automated decisions. Meanwhile, recruiters report a massive surge in applications, with many candidates using AI to polish or write their submissions.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Candidates fear recruitment software introduces bias and lacks human context. Surveys show that many ethnically diverse jobseekers alter their CVs out of fear of rejection. Conversely, recruiters note a perception gap, as candidates believe AI screens CVs far more often than it actually does.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Campaigners and regulators call for greater transparency, audits, and accountability from employers regarding automated hiring systems.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Matilda The Musical celebrated fifteen years since its London debut. The production premiered in Stratford-upon-Avon in 2010 before moving to the West End.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The show became a major theatre success, reaching over twelve million people globally, playing thousands of performances, and winning numerous international awards.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The musical continues its West End run with tickets available until January 2027, alongside a tour across the UK and Ireland.

gist: Julien Laurens interviews PSG winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in a special podcast episode.
They discuss his upbringing, his father, and moves to Napoli and PSG.
The interview also covers his Ballon d'Or contention and teammate Ousmane Dembélé.

sections.heading: What happened

gist: Former rugby player Phil Vickery has taken up bodybuilding at 50.
He won the 2003 Rugby World Cup and earned 73 caps for England.
Vickery uses training to help manage his mental health and probable CTE diagnosis.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Phil Vickery competed in a bodybuilding show in Hull at the age of 50 after a challenge from a friend. He weighed about 99kg on stage, significantly lighter than his playing days.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Vickery has managed personal struggles and a diagnosis for probable CTE since retiring from rugby. Bodybuilding has provided him with discipline, a goal, and support for his physical and mental wellbeing.

gist: Verstappen complained about severe bumps at the Austin track affecting drivers' spines.
Norris supported Verstappen's concerns, while Russell viewed the bumps as part of racing.
Current regulations make cars run lower in corners, worsening the bumpy conditions.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Drivers raised concerns about severe bumps at the Austin track, with Verstappen reporting extreme vertical loads impacting his spine. Norris agreed that the track is very bumpy and causes headaches, while Russell considered the bumps a normal part of racing.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The track conditions cause physical strain and potential damage to drivers' spines and health. Current car regulations exacerbate the problem by forcing cars to run lower in corners, raising safety and comfort issues.

fivew: Verstappen, Lando Norris, and George Russell
Drivers discussed extreme track bumps and physical strain at Austin.
The track surface and car regulations create severe vertical loads.
